1. Core Clinical Tension: A 52-year-old woman with insulin-dependent diabetes presents with chronic neuropathic hand pain and 11-20 well-defined hypochromic and erythematous skin lesions with localized hypoesthesia, easily misattributed to diabetic distal sensory polyneuropathy or diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy. Furthermore, slit-skin smear bacilloscopy was negative, creating a diagnostic challenge in differentiating diabetic mononeuritis multiplex from paucibacillary borderline tuberculoid Hansen's disease with reversal reaction.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The point of initial outpatient clinical presentation and neurological/dermatological physical exam (documenting 11-20 hypochromic/erythematous lesions, left arm hypoesthesia, and bilateral ulnar nerve thickening with focal sensorimotor deficit), immediately prior to skin biopsy histopathology and slit-skin smear bacilloscopy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Diabetic neuropathy typically causes symmetric, length-dependent distal polyneuropathy or acute lumbosacral plexopathy without well-circumscribed hypoesthetic cutaneous plaques; borderline tuberculoid leprosy classically causes asymmetrical peripheral nerve trunk enlargement coinciding with discrete hypoesthetic/anesthetic cutaneous macules and dermal epithelioid granulomas.
case_prompt:
A 52-year-old female residing in the metropolitan region of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, presented to an outpatient specialty clinic with a 1-year history of persistent skin lesions and progressive neuropathic pain in both hands. Her past medical history was notable for insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus managed with NPH and regular insulin under good endocrinologic control, dyslipidemia, and a 35 pack-year smoking history. She reported having had contact with a sibling who had suffered from a chronic granulomatous skin and nerve disease, although there was no family history of hereditary neuropathy.

Physical and dermatological examination revealed 11 to 20 well-defined, erythematous and hypochromic macules and plaques distributed across her body, with objective hypoesthesia detected specifically over a cutaneous lesion on the left upper limb.

Neurological assessment revealed prominent bilateral thickening of the ulnar nerves at the level of the elbow groove. Sensory testing showed thermal and pinprick hypoesthesia in the right ulnar nerve distribution, and tactile hypoesthesia with complete thermal and pain insensitivity in the left ulnar nerve distribution. Motor evaluation revealed asymmetric muscle weakness (Medical Research Council grade 4/5) in the left hypothenar muscles, specifically affecting the abductor digiti minimi and first dorsal interosseous muscles. No deficits were detected in other nerve territories on initial bedside examination.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given the patient's long-standing insulin-dependent diabetes; however, the presence of discrete, well-defined hypochromic cutaneous plaques with localized intracutaneous sensory loss, alongside palpable supraepicondylar ulnar nerve thickening, is pathognomonic of an infectious/granulomatous etiology rather than metabolic polyneuropathy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Physical and dermatological examination showed 11-20 well-defined, erythematous, and hypochromic lesions, with a hypoesthetic lesion in the left upper limb.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Idiopathic Cubital Tunnel Syndrome / Compressive Ulnar Neuropathy
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to neuropathic pain and weakness in the hypothenar muscles; ruled out by bilateral involvement, co-occurring anesthetic cutaneous macules, and absence of mechanical entrapment on ultrasound.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: At this time, the neurological assessment showed bilateral thickening of the ulnar nerves at the level of the elbow, thermal and painful hypoesthesia in the right ulnar nerve, and tactile hypoesthesia and thermal and pain insensitivity in the left ulnar nerve.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Borderline Tuberculoid Leprosy with Type 1 Reversal Reaction
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Although slit-skin bacilloscopy was negative (characteristic of paucibacillary infection), the diagnosis was confirmed by skin biopsy showing epithelioid granulomas in the dermis consistent with borderline tuberculoid leprosy undergoing a type 1 reversal reaction, and electrophysiology confirming bilateral ulnar myelin and secondary axonal neuropathy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Bacilloscopy was negative and skin biopsy revealed epithelioid granuloma in the dermis compatible with a reversal reaction (type 1). MDT for paucibacillary (PB) leprosy was started after it was classified as borderline tuberculoid (BT).

editor_comments: Zero spoilers in case presentation; breakpoint established prior to bacilloscopy and skin biopsy. Verbatim quotes validated.
